hero.headline: Supreme Court rules against Verizon and AT&T in FCC fine dispute
hero.body:
The Supreme Court rejected constitutional challenges from Verizon and AT&T to more than $100 million in combined fines imposed by the Federal Communications Commission in an 8-1 decision on Thursday.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion, ruling that the companies are not entitled to a jury trial to contest the penalties. The fines relate to how the telecommunications companies handled customer location data.

The case centered on whether the Seventh Amendment's guarantee of jury trials in civil cases applies to FCC enforcement actions. Verizon and AT&T argued that fines of this magnitude entitled them to have a jury evaluate the evidence and determine appropriate penalties. The Supreme Court disagreed with this interpretation, affirming the FCC's regulatory authority to impose financial penalties through administrative processes.

The decision significantly strengthens the FCC's enforcement capabilities and establishes an important precedent for how federal regulatory agencies can impose penalties on companies under their jurisdiction. The ruling confirms that agencies can continue using administrative procedures rather than jury trials when levying fines for violations of regulations they oversee.

Only one justice dissented from the majority opinion. The court has not yet released details about which justice broke from the majority or the specific reasoning behind the dissent.

This ruling resolves a legal battle that has worked through the court system as the telecommunications companies sought to overturn or reduce the substantial penalties. The decision represents a significant win for the FCC in defending its enforcement authority against constitutional challenges from major corporations.

The case highlights the ongoing tension between corporate defendants seeking traditional legal protections like jury trials and federal agencies arguing that regulatory matters require specialized administrative proceedings. The Supreme Court's decision favors the regulatory approach, allowing agencies greater flexibility in implementing enforcement actions.

The fines against Verizon and AT&T are among the largest penalties the FCC has levied against telecommunications companies, making this case particularly significant for the industry. The ruling may also have broader implications for how other federal agencies conduct enforcement actions against regulated entities.

The telecommunications companies had argued that the magnitude of the fines—exceeding $100 million combined—warranted the constitutional protections afforded by a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment. However, the Court determined that the FCC's administrative process provided sufficient protection and that jury trials are not required in regulatory enforcement contexts.

This decision gives the FCC and potentially other federal agencies more certainty in pursuing enforcement actions. Companies challenging future regulatory fines will face an uphill legal battle in arguing that jury trials are constitutionally required. The Supreme Court has effectively endorsed the modern administrative state's approach to regulating major corporations in specialized areas like telecommunications.

cards.headline: House votes to block further military action against Iran as Trump attacks Republicans who backed measure
cards.body:
The House of Representatives passed a measure seeking to halt additional military action against Iran, delivering a rebuke to President Trump. The vote took place after the United States conducted strikes on Iranian targets, though the resolution is considered largely symbolic and faces an uncertain path in the Senate.

Trump responded by calling Republicans who voted for the measure "bad" and "unpatriotic." The president's public attacks on members of his own party highlight growing tension within the Republican caucus over the administration's handling of military operations in Iran. The lower chamber's vote represents a rare instance of congressional pushback against presidential war powers, even as many observers question whether the measure will lead to any practical constraints on military action.

The United States announced a ceasefire agreement with Lebanon on Wednesday night following talks aimed at reducing tensions in the region. However, Hezbollah rejected the renewed ceasefire that Israel and Lebanon had agreed to, complicating diplomatic efforts. The U.N. peacekeeping mission for Lebanon reported that one peacekeeper was killed and others were wounded when they came under mortar fire in southeastern Lebanon, underscoring the volatile security situation.

The House vote follows a pattern of congressional efforts to reassert authority over decisions about military force. War powers resolutions typically require the president to withdraw forces from hostilities unless Congress authorizes continued military action. However, presidents of both parties have historically challenged the constitutionality of such measures and often continued operations despite congressional objections.

The split within the Republican Party over Iran policy could complicate Trump's ability to maintain unified support for his foreign policy agenda. Republicans who broke ranks faced immediate criticism from the president, a tactic Trump has used throughout his presidency to pressure party members into alignment. The measure's symbolic nature means military operations can continue in the near term, but the vote signals that some lawmakers are willing to challenge the administration on national security decisions despite potential political consequences.

cards.headline: Blackstone Caps Withdrawals From Flagship Private Credit Fund
cards.body:
Blackstone has restricted withdrawals from its flagship private credit fund as redemption requests surged to concerning levels. The investment firm implemented caps on withdrawals after clients sought to pull money from the Cliffwater Private Credit Fund, highlighting mounting anxiety in the $2 trillion private credit sector.

The restriction comes as the Financial Stability Board, a global watchdog monitoring financial authorities across 24 countries, raised alarm over risks embedded in the private credit market. The board warned that a sharp correction in asset valuations could trigger "sizeable" losses for private credit investors, particularly given heavy exposure to the artificial intelligence sector.

Private credit firms have become major lenders to AI companies seeking to finance datacentres and related infrastructure. AI industry deals now account for more than a third of private credit transactions in 2025, up dramatically from 17% over the previous five years. This concentration poses significant risks. The FSB cautioned that a critical electricity supply shortfall could delay or cancel datacentre projects, while an oversupply of datacentres might outpace demand for AI services and deliver lower-than-expected returns.

The private credit industry has grown rapidly as institutional investors and wealthy individuals pursue higher returns than traditional bonds offer. These funds lend directly to companies, often those unable to access public debt markets. Investments typically involve extended lockup periods, making sudden withdrawal requests difficult to manage without affecting fund performance.

Concerns about the sector intensified following high-profile corporate failures. Two private credit-backed US automotive companies, Tricolor and First Brands, collapsed last year amid fraud allegations. The failures raised questions about whether private lenders had been sufficiently rigorous in evaluating borrower creditworthiness. Major banks including JPMorgan Chase and Barclays sustained losses from Tricolor's failure, while UBS and Jefferies reported significant exposure to both failures.

The FSB report noted that private credit borrowers typically carry lower credit scores and larger debt loads compared with companies using traditional bank financing. Banks now face expanding exposure to the opaque private credit sector through direct lending to funds, financing riskier portfolios, and lending to firms simultaneously borrowing from private credit providers. An increasing number of banks are partnering with asset managers on private credit deals.

When multiple investors attempt to exit private asset funds simultaneously, fund managers may need to sell holdings rapidly at unfavorable prices. This dynamic proves particularly problematic in less liquid markets like private credit, where assets cannot be sold as easily as publicly traded securities. Blackstone's decision to cap redemptions aims to manage outflows methodically rather than trigger forced asset sales that could roil markets and harm remaining investors.

The restriction signals ongoing tension between offering investment flexibility and preserving fund stability in alternative asset markets.

cards.headline: Weekly Jobless Claims Rise to 225,000, Highest Since February
cards.teaser: Unemployment insurance filings increased during a holiday week but remain at historically healthy levels.
cards.body:
Initial jobless claims rose to 225,000 last week, the highest level since February but still indicating a stable labor market. The increase came during a week affected by holidays, which can create volatility in weekly employment data.

The filings for unemployment benefits, used as a measure of layoffs, rose more than economists expected. Despite the increase, the level remains historically low and suggests the labor market continues to hold up. Gold prices rose above $4,500 per ounce following the release of the jobless claims data.

cards.headline: Flesh-eating screwworm parasite confirmed in U.S. cattle
cards.teaser: The deadly parasite has been found in Texas, raising concerns for the cattle industry.
cards.body:
The New World screwworm fly has been confirmed in a calf in Texas, marking the first case in U.S. cattle in six decades, according to agriculture officials. The infected animal was found in south Texas, approximately 50 miles from the Mexico border.

The parasitic fly larvae feed on living tissue of warm-blooded animals, causing significant concern for the American livestock industry. The reemergence of this once-eradicated parasite threatens cattle herds across the country and could have serious economic consequences for ranchers and the cattle industry.

cards.headline: SpaceX Prepares for Public Offering With Updated Prospectus
cards.teaser: Elon Musk's space company released a prospectus showing confidence in its planned market debut, though some analysts see risks.
cards.body:
SpaceX filed an updated prospectus ahead of its planned initial public offering, revealing details about the company's path to going public. The document underscores the confidence of Elon Musk's aerospace firm in its market debut, though some market observers have raised concerns about the offering.

Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and chief operating officer, has been described as a stabilizing force at the company as it prepares for the blockbuster IPO. Her operational leadership contrasts with Musk's more public-facing role, providing what sources characterize as steady management during the transition to public markets.

cards.headline: Hezbollah Rejects Ceasefire Between Israel and Lebanon
cards.teaser: Hezbollah rejected a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon that the United States announced on Wednesday night.
cards.body:
The United States announced a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon on Wednesday night following fresh diplomatic talks. However, Hezbollah, the Iran-backed group that was excluded from the U.S.-brokered negotiations, rejected the deal through its leader and said it would not honor the agreement.

Fighting continued after the ceasefire announcement, with Israel and Hezbollah exchanging strikes. A U.N. peacekeeper was killed and others wounded when they came under mortar fire in southeastern Lebanon. The exclusion of Hezbollah—a major military and political force operating in southern Lebanon—raises questions about the ceasefire's effectiveness on the ground.

hero.headline: Gun Battles Erupt in Mogadishu as Political Rivals Clash
hero.teaser: Armed groups loyal to rival politicians fought in Somalia's capital in what residents described as the worst violence in years.
hero.body:
Fighting broke out in Mogadishu on Thursday as armed groups supporting different politicians engaged in gun battles. Residents said the clashes represented the most intense fighting the capital had seen in years.

The violence comes amid tensions over election delays in Somalia. The president's term in office was recently extended by a year, and the opposition has called for protests against the move. Heavy gunfire was reported across the capital as the political dispute escalated into armed conflict.

cards.headline: Marjane Satrapi, Author of Persepolis, Dies at 56
cards.teaser: The graphic novelist known for her memoir of growing up during the Islamic Revolution in Iran has died.
cards.body:
Marjane Satrapi, the French-Iranian author and illustrator best known for her graphic novel series Persepolis, has died at age 56. The acclaimed memoir, published in the early 2000s, followed a girl's experiences growing up in Iran during the Islamic Revolution and the Iran-Iraq War. The work gained international recognition and helped reshape perceptions of Iran worldwide.

According to her family, Satrapi died of sadness following the death of her husband, Swedish producer Mattias Ripa, last year. Beyond her graphic novels, she was also recognized as a filmmaker—Persepolis was adapted into an Oscar-nominated film.

cards.headline: Ebola Death of Priest Spreads Fear in Congolese Town
cards.teaser: A priest's death from Ebola has raised concerns in a town in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
cards.body:
The death of a priest from Ebola has created fear and uncertainty in a Congolese town. The case has stirred concern among residents about the spread of the disease in the community.

Ebola outbreaks have periodically affected parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with the disease spreading through close contact with infected individuals. The death of a prominent community figure like a priest often heightens public anxiety about transmission risks.

cards.headline: Ukraine Accused of Killing Four in Occupied Crimea
cards.teaser: Russian-backed officials say at least 10 people were injured in attacks they attribute to Ukraine.
cards.body:
Four people were killed in occupied Crimea in attacks that Russian-backed officials attributed to Ukraine. At least 10 others were injured in the strikes, according to the officials.

Crimea has been under Russian occupation since 2014, and the peninsula has periodically been the site of attacks during the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Russian-backed authorities in the territory blamed Ukrainian forces for the deaths.

cards.headline: Charges Dropped Against Budapest Mayor Over Pride March
cards.teaser: Budapest's liberal mayor had faced charges for helping organize a banned 2025 Pride march.
cards.body:
Charges against Budapest Mayor Gergely Karacsony have been dropped. The liberal mayor had faced charges related to organizing the 2025 Pride march, which authorities had banned.

Karacsony has been a prominent opposition voice in Hungary, where the government maintains restrictive policies toward LGBTQ rights and events. The dismissal of charges concludes a legal case that highlighted the ongoing conflict between the national government and Budapest's leadership.

cards.headline: Colombian Presidential Candidate Accused of Co-opting Soccer Jersey
cards.teaser: A candidate endorsed by President Trump faces criticism for using Colombia's yellow national team jersey as a political symbol.
cards.body:
A presidential candidate in Colombia has been accused of turning the national soccer team's yellow jersey into a political statement. The candidate, Abelardo De La Espriella, has been endorsed by President Trump ahead of Colombia's presidential runoff.

The yellow jersey has traditionally been a symbol of national unity in Colombia, worn by the beloved national soccer team. Some Colombians say De La Espriella, a dual citizen of Colombia and the United States, has inappropriately politicized the iconic garment for his campaign.

cards.headline: Hezbollah rejects ceasefire agreement reached by Israel and Lebanon
cards.teaser: The United States announced the ceasefire agreement following a fresh round of talks.
cards.body:
Hezbollah has rejected a ceasefire agreement that Israel and Lebanon reached following U.S.-brokered talks announced Wednesday night. The rejection raises questions about the prospects for de-escalating the conflict.

Violence continued despite the diplomatic initiative. The U.N. peacekeeping force in Lebanon reported that one peacekeeper was killed and several others wounded when they came under mortar fire in southeastern Lebanon.

cards.headline: Marjane Satrapi, Oscar-nominated Persepolis author, dies at 56
cards.teaser: The French-Iranian author and illustrator was known for her graphic novel series and film.
cards.body:
Marjane Satrapi, the French-Iranian author and illustrator behind the acclaimed graphic novel series Persepolis, has died at age 56. Her landmark memoir reshaped international perceptions of Iran through her distinctive artistic style and storytelling.

According to her family, Satrapi died of sadness following the death of her husband, Swedish producer Mattias Ripa, last year. The Persepolis film adaptation earned an Oscar nomination, cementing her place as a prominent voice in contemporary graphic literature.

cards.headline: Gun control group sues federal agencies over crime gun seller records
cards.teaser: Brady filed suit against the ATF and Justice Department for refusing to release information.
cards.body:
Brady, a nonprofit gun control advocacy group, is suing the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Department of Justice. The lawsuit targets the agencies' refusal to release documents and information identifying the largest sellers of crime guns in the United States.

The organization is seeking access to records that would reveal which firearms dealers are associated with guns used in crimes. The legal action follows the federal agencies' decision to withhold the requested information.

cards.headline: Obama presidential museum opens this month with $850 million facility
cards.teaser: The center includes books, exhibits, and a beehive among its features.
cards.body:
The Obama Presidential Center is set to open this month as a museum dedicated to Barack Obama's presidency. The facility cost $850 million to construct and represents a new approach to presidential museums.

The center includes a collection of books, exhibits documenting Obama's presidency, and features such as a beehive. The museum offers visitors an opportunity to explore the history and legacy of the 44th president through various displays and interactive elements.

cards.headline: Man admits violent disorder at Henry Nowak protest
cards.teaser: Disorder occurred in Southampton near the home of Henry Nowak's murderer.
cards.body:
A man admitted to charges of violent disorder at a protest in Southampton on Tuesday night near the home of Henry Nowak's convicted murderer.

The case has attracted international attention from far-right politicians across Europe, who have used clips of Nowak's death to make claims about immigration and race. Prime Minister Keir Starmer accused X owner Elon Musk of attempting to stoke division over the murder after Musk posted criticism of police handling on the social media platform. Nowak's family had appealed for the public not to exploit the killing for political purposes and to focus instead on tackling knife crime.

cards.headline: Quantinuum Raises $1.68 Billion in Quantum Computing IPO
cards.teaser: The Honeywell-backed quantum computing company priced its initial public offering at $60 per share and began trading.
cards.body:
Quantinuum, a quantum computing company backed by Honeywell, raised $1.68 billion in its initial public offering. The company priced shares at $60 each and began trading on public markets, with the offering larger than originally planned.

The IPO marks a milestone for the quantum computing industry's transition to public markets. It reflects growing investor confidence in quantum technology's potential to tackle complex computational problems that traditional computers cannot solve.

cards.headline: Stock Markets Split as Dow Gains 500 Points, Nasdaq Falls After Broadcom Earnings
cards.teaser: Major indexes moved in opposite directions as investors rotated out of chip stocks and into banks and retail.
cards.body:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped more than 500 points while the Nasdaq declined following Broadcom's earnings announcement. The divergence reflected a significant shift in investor positioning, as money flowed out of semiconductor stocks into other sectors.

Broadcom's earnings report sparked a pullback in chip stocks that pressured the technology-heavy Nasdaq. The market rotation showed investors favoring traditional economy stocks over technology shares at this time.

cards.headline: Global Stock Rally Creates 2 Million New Millionaires
cards.teaser: Rising equity markets, driven partly by artificial intelligence enthusiasm, minted millionaires at the fastest pace in four years.
cards.body:
Stock market gains worldwide added approximately 2 million new millionaires last year. The surge was driven largely by artificial intelligence-related investments, which fueled significant equity market growth.

The United States saw millionaire creation accelerate to its fastest pace in four years, reflecting broader wealth expansion. The rally has contributed to widening disparities in wealth distribution, with those holding substantial stock portfolios benefiting most from the market gains.

cards.headline: Pace Gallery Cuts 50 Artists and 50 Staff Members
cards.teaser: The established art gallery is contracting as the art market faces ongoing challenges.
cards.body:
Pace Gallery reduced its roster by 50 artists and eliminated 50 staff positions as the art market continues to face economic pressures. The cuts at the well-established gallery reflect broader difficulties in the contemporary art market.

Even established players in the art world are being forced to contract their operations. The reductions affect both the gallery's representation of artists and its internal workforce, signaling that market challenges are affecting multiple aspects of the business.

hero.headline: Meteorite found in Sahara may preserve evidence of lost early planet
hero.body:
A meteorite discovered in the Sahara Desert appears to contain the first physical evidence of a planetary body that existed in the early solar system but no longer survives. The rare fragment suggests the solar system may have once included an additional rocky planet that was destroyed or ejected billions of years ago.

Researchers analyzing the meteorite's composition identified characteristics that do not match any known asteroid or planetary body currently in the solar system. The fragment's chemical signature points to a parent body with properties similar to terrestrial planets like Earth and Mars, but with distinct differences that indicate it came from a separate world. Scientists believe this parent body likely formed during the chaotic early period of solar system formation, when collisions between growing planets were common.

The discovery adds to growing evidence that the solar system's current configuration does not represent its original state. Computer models of planetary formation have long predicted that additional planets may have formed in the inner solar system before being destroyed through violent collisions or gravitational interactions. Until now, however, direct physical evidence of such lost worlds has remained elusive.

Meteorites provide scientists with samples of material from the early solar system that would otherwise be impossible to study. Most meteorites come from the asteroid belt, which contains fragments of objects that never grew large enough to become full planets. This particular specimen appears to represent something different: debris from a body that did achieve planetary size before meeting a catastrophic end.

The findings could reshape understanding of how the solar system evolved into its present form. If confirmed, the meteorite would represent the only known remnant of a lost planet, offering a rare window into the violent processes that shaped the worlds we see today. Researchers continue to analyze the fragment's isotopic composition and mineral structure to learn more about the conditions on this ancient world before its destruction.

The discovery has generated significant interest across the scientific community, with multiple outlets covering the findings. Researchers emphasize that further analysis is needed to fully confirm the meteorite's origins and what it reveals about early solar system dynamics. The work demonstrates how individual fragments recovered from Earth's deserts can provide crucial insights into planetary formation and the history of our cosmic neighborhood.

cards.headline: Geomagnetic storm watch upgraded for northern lights across 25 states
cards.teaser: Federal forecasters upgraded the watch to G3 level, indicating strong geomagnetic storm conditions that could push aurora visibility farther south than usual.
cards.body:
A geomagnetic storm watch has been upgraded to G3 level, with northern lights expected to be visible across 25 states including Vermont, New York, and New Hampshire. The severe alert indicates strong geomagnetic activity capable of pushing aurora displays farther south than usual.

G3-level storms can disrupt power grids and satellite operations while producing vivid aurora displays visible to the naked eye. The watch covers the period of June 4-5 UTC.

cards.headline: Oura releases Ring 5, 40 percent smaller than previous model
cards.teaser: The company describes the Ring 5 as the world's smallest smart ring, with significant size reduction while maintaining health tracking capabilities.
cards.body:
Oura introduced the Ring 5, marketing it as the world's smallest smart ring at 40 percent smaller than its predecessor. The device starts at $399 and delivers the same health monitoring capabilities as earlier versions, including sleep tracking and activity measurement.

The Ring 5 is both thinner and lighter than the previous generation. Oura has announced new software features rolling out to help users monitor their health metrics more proactively, with additional durability and battery life details expected to emerge as testing progresses.

cards.headline: Apple reports $1.4 trillion in App Store transactions, most without commission
cards.teaser: The company said 90 percent of the billing and sales on its platform occurred without Apple collecting a commission.
cards.body:
Apple's App Store generated $1.4 trillion in total billings and sales, up from $1.3 trillion the previous year. Digital goods and services accounted for $149 billion of that figure.

The company highlighted that 90 percent of App Store transactions occurred without Apple taking a commission, a statistic the company has emphasized amid regulatory scrutiny over its commission structure across multiple jurisdictions.

cards.headline: Google releases Fitbit Air specifications for third-party accessories
cards.teaser: The company published CAD drawings and technical specifications allowing anyone to design and manufacture bands and accessories for the Fitbit Air.
cards.body:
Google released complete technical specifications and CAD drawings for the Fitbit Air, opening the device to third-party accessory makers. The blueprints include precise measurements and design guidelines, enabling individuals and manufacturers to create custom bands and other accessories. The company specifically noted that bicep bands are now supported configurations.

The release allows for 3D printing of custom accessories and gives accessory makers official specifications to work from. Google published the technical documents and guidelines through official channels, marking a shift toward greater openness in its wearable device ecosystem.

cards.headline: Waymo begins repurposing robotaxi batteries for power grid storage
cards.teaser: Used batteries from the autonomous vehicle fleet will be deployed in energy storage projects in California and Texas.
cards.body:
Waymo announced it will repurpose batteries from its robotaxi fleet for use in electrical grid storage systems. The used batteries will support energy storage projects in California and Texas, extending the useful life of the components beyond their automotive applications.

The initiative addresses both battery disposal concerns and grid-scale energy storage needs. Batteries that no longer meet the performance requirements for autonomous vehicles can still provide sufficient capacity for stationary energy storage applications, where weight and space constraints are less critical than in vehicles.

cards.headline: Ace Combat 8 set for October release on PlayStation 5
cards.teaser: The aerial combat game launches globally on October 2, with gameplay that explores themes of heroism and misinformation.
cards.body:
Bandai Namco announced that Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve will launch worldwide on October 2 for PlayStation 5. The game continues the series' focus on aerial dogfighting while incorporating themes about misinformation and the nature of heroism in combat scenarios.

Preview coverage highlighted the game's cloud systems, which function as tactical combat tools rather than purely visual elements. The eighth mainframe entry in the series asks players to take on heroic roles while questioning whether their actions align with that characterization. Military.com noted the game's attention to realistic aerial combat mechanics.

hero.headline: Russell Wilson retires from NFL, joins CBS Sports as broadcaster
hero.body:
Russell Wilson has announced his retirement from professional football after 14 seasons, marking the end of a career that included a Super Bowl championship and multiple Pro Bowl selections. The former quarterback will join CBS Sports as an analyst on The NFL Today, the network's flagship pregame show.

Wilson's wife, singer Ciara, shared an emotional message following the retirement announcement. The quarterback posted a video titled "thank you, football" to make his transition official.

The decision to step away from playing has sparked considerable debate about Wilson's Hall of Fame credentials. While his resume includes a Super Bowl win with the Seattle Seahawks, 10 Pro Bowl selections, and the Walter Payton Man of the Year Award, analysts are divided on whether these accomplishments make him a surefire Hall of Famer or represent a more typical career arc for a successful quarterback.

Wilson led the Seahawks to a Super Bowl victory and appeared in back-to-back championship games during the 2013 and 2014 seasons. He was known for his dual-threat ability as both a passer and runner. After spending the majority of his career in Seattle, he played for other teams before finishing his playing days with the New York Giants.

Kyle Long, a retired offensive lineman, will also join The NFL Today alongside Wilson. The addition of the two former players represents a notable change to CBS's NFL broadcast team as the network continues to rebuild its coverage personnel.

The move into broadcasting allows Wilson to remain connected to football while stepping back from the physical demands of playing. CBS has been actively reshaping its NFL coverage, and Wilson's recent playing experience combined with his high profile are expected to attract viewers to the network's programming.

Wilson's Hall of Fame discussion reflects broader questions about quarterback legacies. While his 10 Pro Bowl selections and Super Bowl victory are significant achievements, some analysts question whether his overall body of work meets the standard for induction into professional football's highest honor. Others view his career as solid and successful but not exceptional enough to guarantee enshrinement.

The discussion around Wilson's Hall of Fame case remains complex and multifaceted. His accomplishments are substantial, yet the football community has not reached consensus on where his career ranks among all-time greats. This uncertainty mirrors the diverse perspectives on what defines a Hall of Fame-caliber quarterback.

Wilson's first appearance on The NFL Today has not yet been scheduled. His transition from player to analyst marks another chapter in a career that has kept him in the public eye throughout his time in professional football.

cards.headline: Knicks take Game 1 of NBA Finals behind Jalen Brunson
cards.teaser: Jalen Brunson led a late surge as the Knicks defeated the Spurs in the opening game of the NBA Finals in San Antonio.
cards.body:
The New York Knicks defeated the San Antonio Spurs 105-95 in Game 1 of the NBA Finals, taking a 1-0 series lead on the road. Jalen Brunson led the way with 30 points, delivering a dominant performance that helped the Knicks maintain their remarkable playoff streak.

The game was defensive and low-scoring, with both teams struggling from three-point range. The Knicks held Victor Wembanyama, the Spurs' star player, in check through much of the contest. The victory puts New York just three wins away from capturing their first championship since 1973.

cards.headline: Russian teenager Andreeva reaches first Grand Slam final at French Open
cards.teaser: Mirra Andreeva defeated Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk in straight sets to become the youngest French Open finalist in years.
cards.body:
Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva advanced to her first Grand Slam final by defeating Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk 6-1, 6-3 at the French Open. The dominant performance saw Andreeva control the match throughout, breaking through in major competition with an impressive display.

The victory marks a significant breakthrough for the young Russian player on the Grand Slam stage. Andreeva will now compete for the French Open championship in what represents a major milestone in her tennis career.

cards.headline: Patriots acquire A.J. Brown from Eagles in blockbuster trade
cards.teaser: The New England Patriots traded for wide receiver A.J. Brown, prompting strong reactions from both organizations.
cards.body:
The New England Patriots acquired wide receiver A.J. Brown in a trade with the Philadelphia Eagles. Eagles left tackle Jordan Mailata expressed relief after the trade, stating "thank God it's over," while reactions at Eagles organized team activities were mixed.

A Patriots defensive tackle made a strong statement following the acquisition. The trade carries risk for New England, but the team is demonstrating a commitment to winning. The Eagles are moving forward without one of their top offensive weapons.

cards.headline: England collapse to 55-5 on opening day of first Test against New Zealand
cards.teaser: England suffered a disastrous start at Lord's, losing five wickets for just 55 runs against New Zealand.
cards.body:
England's opening day at Lord's proved disastrous as they collapsed to 55-5 against New Zealand in the first Test. The home side's top order struggled badly against the visitors' bowling attack, with Kyle Jamieson proving particularly effective.

Wicketkeeper Jamie Smith's dismissal epitomized England's troubles. Facing Jamieson, Smith elected to leave a delivery that caught him unaware, only to be bowled for just one run—a decision he will want to forget quickly. The early loss of Emilio Gay, who managed eight runs on his Test debut before being caught off Jamieson's bowling at 16-1, set the tone for a difficult day.

cards.headline: Browns edge rusher Jared Verse discusses role alongside Carson Schwesinger
cards.teaser: Jared Verse said he can play with more freedom knowing linebacker Carson Schwesinger is behind him in Cleveland's defense.
cards.body:
Cleveland Browns edge rusher Jared Verse said he can play more freely with linebacker Carson Schwesinger supporting him in the defensive scheme. Verse, who was traded to Cleveland from the Los Angeles Rams, emphasized he is not trying to replace Myles Garrett, who was dealt to the Rams in the same transaction.

Verse expressed that joining the Browns feels like home and discussed his excitement about forming a defensive tandem with Schwesinger. The pairing represents a new chapter for Cleveland's defense following the departure of Garrett.

cards.headline: Tottenham expected to increase bid for Brighton defender Van Hecke
cards.teaser: Brighton rejected an initial 70 million pound offer from Tottenham for Netherlands defender Jan Paul van Hecke.
cards.body:
Brighton are expecting Tottenham to submit an increased offer for defender Jan Paul van Hecke after rejecting the club's initial bid of £70 million. The Dutch international has become a key player in Brighton's defense, and the rejection suggests the club values him significantly higher than Spurs' opening proposal.

Tottenham's continued pursuit indicates they see Van Hecke as an important target to bolster their backline.

hero.headline: Marjane Satrapi, Oscar-Nominated Persepolis Creator, Dies at 56
hero.body:
Marjane Satrapi, the French-Iranian artist, filmmaker and graphic novelist whose acclaimed memoir Persepolis reshaped international perceptions of Iran, has died at age 56. Her family stated that she had "died of sadness" following the death of her husband, Swedish producer Mattias Ripa, who passed away in April of the previous year. Messages posted on her Instagram account later that month included the phrase: "For I lost the love of my life."

Born in 1969 in Rasht, Iran, Satrapi was raised in Tehran by her father, an engineer, and her mother, a dress designer. As a teenager, her parents sent her to Europe to continue her education and escape the restrictions of the Islamic Republic. She eventually settled in France, arriving in 1994 and becoming a French citizen in 2006.

Satrapi achieved international recognition in 2000 with Persepolis, a graphic novel memoir that became a publishing phenomenon. The work told the story of a rebellious young girl navigating Iran's upheaval after the 1979 revolution and the establishment of the Islamic Republic. It followed her journey until she was sent alone to Europe at age 14. The memoir sold millions of copies and established Satrapi as one of the most widely read Iranian authors worldwide.

Satrapi has said she initially had minimal expectations for the work. "With Persepolis, I didn't even think I'd find a publisher," she told El País in 2020. "I thought I'd make 50 photocopies for my friends to read."

The animated film adaptation, which Satrapi co-directed, became an international success and earned her a historic place as the first woman nominated for the Academy Award for best animated feature. She also won the Jury Prize at the Cannes Film Festival for the film.

Beyond comics, Satrapi directed five feature films, including Radioactive in 2019, starring Rosamund Pike as Marie Curie. After stepping away from comics for years, she returned to the medium in 2024 with Woman, Life, Freedom, a collaborative graphic work bringing together 17 Iranian and international comic artists. The book examined the protest movement that emerged after Mahsa Amini's death in custody in 2022.

President Emmanuel Macron paid tribute to Satrapi, calling her "a great artist who turned her Iranian childhood into a universal tale." Yaël Braun-Pivet, president of the French National Assembly, noted that "Marjane Satrapi had turned her work into an act of freedom" and carried forward the fight for women's freedom and dignity. Her work challenged Western assumptions about Iranian society and gave voice to young Iranians facing government restrictions.

cards.headline: CBS News Fires Scott Pelley, Conducts Layoffs and Shuts Down Radio Operation
cards.teaser: CBS News terminated correspondent Scott Pelley, conducted layoffs, and shut down CBS News Radio in moves that drew sharp criticism from the Writers Guild of America East.
cards.body:
CBS News fired Scott Pelley, a longtime 60 Minutes correspondent, as part of broader cost-cutting measures at the Paramount-owned news division. The company also conducted layoffs and shut down CBS News Radio entirely.

Pelley publicly accused CBS executives of instructing him to "inject falsehoods and bias" into his reporting and of silencing employees. He stated that 60 Minutes' decades-long success as America's top-rated program stems from the integrity and quality of its journalism. The Writers Guild of America East condemned the firings and layoffs as cruel and needless, arguing they demonstrate contempt for the journalism profession.

cards.headline: Olivia Rodrigo Condemns Trump Administration Use of Her Song for ICE Promotions
cards.teaser: Singer Olivia Rodrigo said she was enraged after discovering the Trump White House used her song to promote ICE deportations last fall.
cards.body:
Olivia Rodrigo discovered last fall that the Trump administration's Department of Homeland Security was using her song "All-American Bitch" to promote ICE deportations while scrolling through her phone. The discovery prompted a strong response from the artist, who described the situation as deeply disturbing.

In an interview with Dazed magazine ahead of her third studio album release, Rodrigo criticized both the unauthorized use of her music and the deportation policies themselves. She characterized the administration's actions as "awful, barbaric and cruel."

cards.headline: Paramount Movie Hack Escalates Into Ongoing Crisis
cards.teaser: A cyberattack targeting Paramount has expanded into a wider crisis affecting the studio's operations.
cards.body:
Paramount faced an escalating security crisis following a hack that targeted the studio's movie operations. The Hollywood Reporter reported on how the initial breach spiraled into a broader situation affecting the company.

The incident represents the latest in a series of high-profile cyberattacks affecting major entertainment companies. The scope and impact of the breach continued to develop as the studio worked to address the security compromise.

cards.headline: Ticketmaster Halts Celine Dion Comeback Show Sales Over Suspicious Activity
cards.teaser: Ticketmaster suspended ticket sales for Celine Dion's comeback performances after detecting suspicious activity on its platform.
cards.body:
The live entertainment company stopped ticket sales for Celine Dion's return to performing after identifying suspicious activity during the sale process. Fans had spent hours waiting in online queues before being removed from the system.

The shutdown came as anticipation ran high for Dion's comeback shows. Ticketmaster has not announced when sales might resume or provided details about the nature of the suspicious activity that prompted the halt.

cards.headline: SXSW London Faces Criticism Over Response to Cenk Uygur U.K. Entry Ban
cards.teaser: Broadcaster Piers Morgan criticized SXSW London's handling of the situation after Cenk Uygur and Hasan Piker were barred from entering the United Kingdom.
cards.body:
Piers Morgan said he was disappointed in SXSW London's reaction after broadcaster Cenk Uygur was barred from entering the United Kingdom. Morgan made the comments while speaking at the festival. Uygur and his nephew Hasan Piker, both scheduled to speak at the event, were blocked by the Home Office from entering the country.

Morgan suggested the organization could have stood up more for Uygur following the government decision. Both Uygur and Piker were unable to fulfill their scheduled speaking engagements at SXSW London due to the entry ban.

cards.headline: Prince Estate Announces Rarities Album Spanning Entire Career
cards.teaser: The Prince estate will release Timeless, a collection of previously unreleased recordings from throughout the late artist's career.
cards.body:
The estate of Prince announced plans to release Timeless, an album of rarities spanning the musician's entire career. The legendary Vault containing Prince's unreleased recordings holds so much material that a deluxe boxed set focused solely on his 1987 album Sign O the Times contained eight CDs without including even half of that album's outtakes.

hero.headline: Supreme Court rules against Verizon and AT&T in FCC fine dispute
hero.body:
The Supreme Court rejected constitutional challenges from Verizon and AT&T to more than $100 million in combined fines imposed by the Federal Communications Commission in an 8-1 decision on Thursday.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion, ruling that the companies are not entitled to a jury trial to contest the penalties. The fines relate to how the telecommunications companies handled customer location data.

The case centered on whether the Seventh Amendment's guarantee of jury trials in civil cases applies to FCC enforcement actions. Verizon and AT&T argued that fines of this magnitude entitled them to have a jury evaluate the evidence and determine appropriate penalties. The Supreme Court disagreed with this interpretation, affirming the FCC's regulatory authority to impose financial penalties through administrative processes.

The decision significantly strengthens the FCC's enforcement capabilities and establishes an important precedent for how federal regulatory agencies can impose penalties on companies under their jurisdiction. The ruling confirms that agencies can continue using administrative procedures rather than jury trials when levying fines for violations of regulations they oversee.

Only one justice dissented from the majority opinion. The court has not yet released details about which justice broke from the majority or the specific reasoning behind the dissent.

This ruling resolves a legal battle that has worked through the court system as the telecommunications companies sought to overturn or reduce the substantial penalties. The decision represents a significant win for the FCC in defending its enforcement authority against constitutional challenges from major corporations.

The case highlights the ongoing tension between corporate defendants seeking traditional legal protections like jury trials and federal agencies arguing that regulatory matters require specialized administrative proceedings. The Supreme Court's decision favors the regulatory approach, allowing agencies greater flexibility in implementing enforcement actions.

The fines against Verizon and AT&T are among the largest penalties the FCC has levied against telecommunications companies, making this case particularly significant for the industry. The ruling may also have broader implications for how other federal agencies conduct enforcement actions against regulated entities.

The telecommunications companies had argued that the magnitude of the fines—exceeding $100 million combined—warranted the constitutional protections afforded by a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment. However, the Court determined that the FCC's administrative process provided sufficient protection and that jury trials are not required in regulatory enforcement contexts.

This decision gives the FCC and potentially other federal agencies more certainty in pursuing enforcement actions. Companies challenging future regulatory fines will face an uphill legal battle in arguing that jury trials are constitutionally required. The Supreme Court has effectively endorsed the modern administrative state's approach to regulating major corporations in specialized areas like telecommunications.

cards.headline: Senate begins vote-a-rama on immigration reconciliation package
cards.teaser: The Senate launched into a voting marathon Thursday to advance a budget reconciliation bill funding immigration enforcement agencies.
cards.body:
The Senate began a vote-a-rama Thursday, launching into an extended series of amendment votes as it works toward passing a budget reconciliation package for immigration enforcement funding. The process allows unlimited amendments and can stretch for many hours before final passage.

Republicans are advancing the bill to fund immigration enforcement through the end of Trump's term. The chamber is expected to reach final passage on the reconciliation bill later this week.

cards.headline: Trump approval rating reaches lowest point in polling tracker
cards.teaser: President Trump's net approval rating fell to its lowest level since tracking began in 2009, according to analysis from The Economist.
cards.body:
President Trump's net approval rating dropped to its lowest point ever recorded in The Economist's polling tracker. The outlet has tracked presidential job performance using YouGov survey data since 2009.

The decline comes as the country faces ongoing military action with Iran and sustained high consumer prices. The polling analysis shows the combination of foreign conflict and economic pressures has weighed on public opinion of the president's job performance.

cards.headline: U.S. strike kills two on suspected drug vessel in eastern Pacific
cards.teaser: U.S. Southern Command launched a strike Wednesday on a boat it says was operated by designated terrorist organizations, killing two people.
cards.body:
The U.S. military struck a vessel traveling through the eastern Pacific on Wednesday, resulting in two deaths. U.S. Southern Command said the boat was operated by designated terrorist organizations and that intelligence confirmed the vessel's intent to transfer narcotics.

SouthCom did not specify which terrorist organizations allegedly operated the vessel or provide additional evidence supporting the drug trafficking claim. The strike represents the latest U.S. military action targeting suspected narcotics smuggling operations in the region.

cards.headline: Trump claims California elections being stolen as vote counting continues
cards.teaser: President Trump accused Democrats of trying to steal elections in California as results continue to come in days after voting concluded.
cards.body:
California's governor's race remained unresolved Thursday as election officials continued processing uncounted ballots, a process expected to take days or weeks. British-born conservative pundit Steve Hilton led early results, followed by former US health secretary Xavier Becerra, with billionaire Tom Steyer in third place.

President Trump claimed Democrats are attempting to steal California's elections as results from multiple races remained incomplete. California's extended vote-counting timeline reflects standard state election procedures, not irregularities.

cards.headline: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: Former Biden administration official Deb Haaland secured the Democratic nomination for New Mexico governor.
cards.body:
Deb Haaland, who served in the Biden administration, won the Democratic primary for governor of New Mexico. The victory positions her as the party's nominee in the general election.

If elected, Haaland would become the first female Native American governor in U.S. history. She previously served as a federal official under President Biden before entering the gubernatorial race.

cards.headline: Deadly cattle pest found in Texas after 60-year absence
cards.teaser: The U.S. Department of Agriculture confirmed a case of New World screwworm in Texas, six decades after the parasite was eradicated.
cards.body:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture confirmed the first case of New World screwworm in cattle in six decades, discovered in a calf in south Texas about 50 miles from the Mexico border. The parasitic fly, whose larvae burrow into flesh, had been effectively eradicated from the United States 60 years ago. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced the finding late Wednesday.

The discovery comes at a challenging time for the cattle industry. The U.S. beef herd is currently at its smallest size in 75 years, while retail beef prices have reached record highs. The reemergence of this flesh-eating parasite threatens cattle operations already struggling with reduced herd sizes and elevated production costs.
